title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Muscarinic antagonists. Ipratropium, oxitropium, tiotropium: bronchodilators; caution in prostate enlargement, bladder outflow obstruction, glaucoma.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Biologics. Omalizumab (anti-IgE), mepolizumab and benralizumab (IL-5 pathway), dupilumab (IL-4/13), tezepelumab (anti-TSLP).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inhaled corticosteroids. Beclometasone, budesonide, fluticasone: first-line long-term control; risk of oral thrush.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Long-acting β₂ agonists. Salmeterol, formoterol (and ultra-long-acting) for maintenance, combined with an ICS.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Leukotriene modifiers. Montelukast blocks cysteinyl leukotriene receptors: prophylaxis, exercise-induced bronchospasm.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: PDE inhibitors. Theophylline (narrow window, TDM) and roflumilast (PDE4, COPD).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Short-acting β₂ agonists. Salbutamol, terbutaline, fenoterol: first line for acute attacks and exercise-induced asthma.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: SMART therapy. One ICS-formoterol inhaler (budesonide-formoterol) for maintenance and reliever.

title: T2-high vs T2-low asthma?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: T2-high vs T2-low asthma?
body.back: T2-high: ≥ half of patients, childhood onset, eosinophilic, allergic, high IgE, steroid-responsive. T2-low: Th1/Th17, neutrophils, non-allergic, less steroid-responsive.

title: Classes of bronchodilators?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Classes of bronchodilators?
body.back: β₂ agonists (SABA: salbutamol, terbutaline, fenoterol; LABA: salmeterol, formoterol) and muscarinic antagonists (ipratropium, oxitropium, tiotropium).

title: Indications for SABAs?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Indications for SABAs?
body.back: First line in acute asthma and exacerbations; prevention of exercise-induced asthma.

title: Antimuscarinic adverse effects and cautions?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Antimuscarinic adverse effects and cautions?
body.back: Pharyngeal irritation, paradoxical bronchospasm; caution in prostate enlargement, bladder outflow obstruction, glaucoma.

title: Role and adverse effect of ICS?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Role and adverse effect of ICS?
body.back: First-line long-term control of persistent asthma; oropharyngeal candidiasis (rinse mouth).

title: Theophylline: key clinical points?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Theophylline: key clinical points?
body.back: Non-selective PDE inhibitor; clearance raised by smoking and high-protein diet; many interactions; TDM; avoid in cor pulmonale, heart failure, liver failure; nausea, arrhythmias, insomnia.

title: What is SMART?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is SMART?
body.back: Single maintenance and reliever therapy with one ICS-formoterol inhaler (budesonide/formoterol, mometasone/formoterol), per GINA 2022 and NHLBI 2020.

title: Asthma biologics and targets?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Asthma biologics and targets?
body.back: Omalizumab: IgE. Mepolizumab, benralizumab: IL-5 pathway. Dupilumab: IL-4/13. Tezepelumab: TSLP.

title: Inhaler device types?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Inhaler device types?
body.back: Pressurised metered-dose inhalers (conventional, breath-actuated) ± spacers; dry powder inhalers (single-dose, multidose: Turbuhaler, Diskus); nebulisers (jet, ultrasonic, mesh).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Parent drug. Lipophilic drugs are hard to excrete; oral and partly rectal drugs undergo first-pass metabolism.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pharmacogenetics. CYP2D6, 2C9, 2C19 and NAT2 polymorphisms change drug levels and responses.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: CYP inducers. Speed metabolism: rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, St John's wort, smoking (CYP1A), ethanol (CYP2E1).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: CYP inhibitors. Slow metabolism: erythromycin, ketoconazole, cimetidine, fluoxetine, quinidine, grapefruit juice (CYP3A4).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Phase I. Introduces or unmasks -OH, -NH₂, -SH, mainly via CYP450 in the smooth ER.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Phase II. Conjugation by transferases with glucuronic acid, sulfate, glutathione or acetyl groups.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Excretion. Hydrophilic conjugates leave in urine or bile.

title: Five outcomes of drug metabolism?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Five outcomes of drug metabolism?
body.back: Deactivation (most), activation of prodrugs, detoxification, toxification (paracetamol), change of solubility (lipophilic → hydrophilic).

title: Phase I vs phase II?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Phase I vs phase II?
body.back: Phase I: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis; mostly CYP450; adds/unmasks -OH, -NH₂, -SH. Phase II: conjugation (glucuronide, sulfate, GSH, acetyl) by transferases → highly polar.

title: Six main CYP enzymes and substrates?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Six main CYP enzymes and substrates?
body.back: 1A2 (methylxanthines), 2C9 (S-warfarin, phenytoin), 2C19 (PPIs), 2D6 (~25% of drugs; cardiac, psychiatric), 2E1 (paracetamol, ethanol), 3A4 (50-60% of drugs; CCBs, statins, steroids, benzodiazepines).

title: List CYP inducers and inhibitors.
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: List CYP inducers and inhibitors.
body.back: Inducers: rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, St John's wort, smoking (1A), ethanol (2E1). Inhibitors: erythromycin, ketoconazole, cimetidine, fluoxetine, quinidine, grapefruit juice.

title: Four metaboliser phenotypes?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Four metaboliser phenotypes?
body.back: Poor, intermediate, extensive (normal), ultra-rapid.

title: CYP2D6 and codeine?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: CYP2D6 and codeine?
body.back: Codeine is converted to morphine by CYP2D6: poor metabolisers get no analgesia; ultra-rapid metabolisers risk overdose.

title: Why do warfarin doses vary 20-fold?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Why do warfarin doses vary 20-fold?
body.back: Polymorphisms in VKORC1 (the target; 1639G>A increases sensitivity) and CYP2C9 (metabolism), plus weight and other factors.

title: NAT2 slow acetylators: drugs and frequencies?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: NAT2 slow acetylators: drugs and frequencies?
body.back: Isoniazid, hydralazine, procainamide, dapsone; ~70% Middle Eastern, 50% Caucasian, 25% Asian.

title: Non-CYP oxidation enzymes?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Non-CYP oxidation enzymes?
body.back: Alcohol dehydrogenase, aldehyde dehydrogenase, monoamine oxidase.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Drug-receptor binding. Usually reversible via hydrogen, ionic and van der Waals bonds; occasionally covalent and irreversible.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Competitive antagonist. Reversible at the agonist site: potency falls (EC₅₀ rises), efficacy unchanged (naloxone, propranolol).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Full agonist. Binds and activates the receptor to give the maximal response (e.g. morphine).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inverse agonist. Prefers the inactive state, reduces constitutive activity (nalmefene).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Irreversible antagonist. Covalent binding lowers maximal efficacy (phenoxybenzamine).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Partial agonist. Lower efficacy at full occupancy (e.g. pentazocine, buprenorphine).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Therapeutic index. TD₅₀ / ED₅₀: small for lithium, digoxin, chemotherapy; large for penicillins.

title: Define pharmacology and its two divisions.
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Define pharmacology and its two divisions.
body.back: Study of substances interacting with living systems by chemical processes. Pharmacodynamics: what drugs do to the body. Pharmacokinetics: what the body does to drugs.

title: What properties must a drug have to bind its receptor?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What properties must a drug have to bind its receptor?
body.back: Appropriate size (mostly 100-1,000 Da), charge, shape and atomic composition; complementary 'key-lock' fit; stereochemistry matters.

title: Full agonist, partial agonist, antagonist, inverse agonist?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Full agonist, partial agonist, antagonist, inverse agonist?
body.back: Full: maximal effect (morphine). Partial: lower maximum (pentazocine, buprenorphine). Antagonist: blocks without effect (naloxone). Inverse: reduces basal activity (nalmefene).

title: Affinity vs potency vs efficacy?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Affinity vs potency vs efficacy?
body.back: Affinity: attraction (Kd; lower = higher). Potency: dose for 50% of max (EC₅₀). Efficacy: maximal effect (Emax).

title: Competitive vs irreversible antagonist on the curve?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Competitive vs irreversible antagonist on the curve?
body.back: Competitive: shifts right, EC₅₀ rises, Emax unchanged, surmountable. Irreversible: Emax falls; duration depends on receptor turnover.

title: What are spare receptors?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What are spare receptors?
body.back: Receptors in excess of those needed for maximal response, so Emax is reached without full occupancy.

title: Four receptor families with examples?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Four receptor families with examples?
body.back: Intracellular (steroids, thyroid hormone), enzyme-linked (insulin, EGF), ligand-gated channels (ACh, GABA, 5-HT, glutamate), GPCRs (cAMP, Ca²⁺-IP₃).

title: How do GPCRs desensitise?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: How do GPCRs desensitise?
body.back: Phosphorylation and β-arrestin-mediated endocytosis; then resensitisation or degradation.

title: Therapeutic index and window?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Therapeutic index and window?
body.back: TI = TD₅₀ / ED₅₀. Large TI: penicillins, cephalosporins, allopurinol. Narrow: lithium, digoxin, phenytoin, theophylline, chemotherapy.

title: Causes of variable drug responses?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Causes of variable drug responses?
body.back: Different drug concentrations at the target (age, weight, sex, disease, organ function), different endogenous ligand levels, altered receptor number or coupling.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Absorption interactions. Acid suppressants change pH, motility drugs change transit, cations chelate tetracyclines and quinolones, P-gp inhibitors raise digoxin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Types of PD interaction. Additive (ibuprofen + paracetamol), synergistic (aminoglycoside + penicillin; sedatives + alcohol), antagonistic (naloxone).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Distribution interactions. Displacement from plasma proteins; transporters at the blood-brain and other barriers.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Elimination interactions. Probenecid blocks OAT (longer penicillin half-life); gemfibrozil blocks OATP (more rosuvastatin).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Metabolic interactions. CYP inhibition raises levels quickly; induction lowers them over 1-2 weeks.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pharmacodynamic interactions. One drug modifies the effect of another at the target level.

title: Epidemiology of DDIs?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Epidemiology of DDIs?
body.back: About 17% of US Medicaid patients had > 1 clinically significant DDI; risk rises with age, comorbidity and polypharmacy.

title: Three types of drug interaction by partner?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Three types of drug interaction by partner?
body.back: Drug-drug, drug-food (e.g. alcohol with sedatives), drug-condition (e.g. decongestant in hypertension).

title: Additive, synergistic, antagonistic: examples?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Additive, synergistic, antagonistic: examples?
body.back: Additive: ibuprofen + paracetamol; zidovudine + ganciclovir. Synergistic: aminoglycoside + penicillin; sedatives + alcohol. Antagonistic: naloxone; zidovudine + stavudine.

title: Absorption interactions?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Absorption interactions?
body.back: Gastric pH (PPIs: atazanavir ↓94%), motility (methadone, metoclopramide), chelation (tetracyclines/quinolones + Fe/Al/Mg/Ca), gut P-gp (quinidine raises digoxin).

title: Inhibition vs induction?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Inhibition vs induction?
body.back: Inhibition: fast, raises levels (competitive or mechanism-based, e.g. grapefruit). Induction: via PXR/CAR, 1-2 weeks, lowers levels or raises toxic metabolites.

title: Classic induction interactions?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Classic induction interactions?
body.back: Phenytoin → contraceptive failure; alcohol → more NAPQI from paracetamol; rifampin shortens half-lives; St John's wort lowers many drugs.

title: Transporter interactions?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Transporter interactions?
body.back: Quinidine-loperamide (CNS entry), St John's wort-ciclosporin (MDR1 induction), probenecid-penicillin (OAT), gemfibrozil-rosuvastatin (OATP), cimetidine (OCT).

title: How do you judge whether a DDI matters?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: How do you judge whether a DDI matters?
body.back: Therapeutic window of the affected drug, number of metabolic routes, alternatives with different susceptibility, patient age and organ function.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Approval. Safety and efficacy must be defined before legal marketing.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Discovery. Identify the target, design or screen molecules, optimise by structure-activity relationship.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Phase 1. 20-100 usually healthy volunteers; safety, dose-finding and pharmacokinetics; months to a year.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Phase 2. 100-300 patients; efficacy (proof of concept) and safety; highest failure rate, only 25% continue.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Phase 3. Hundreds to thousands of patients, multicentre, usually double-blind against the standard treatment.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Phase 4. After approval: long-term benefits, side effects and best use; rare toxicities emerge.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Preclinical testing. In vitro and animal studies: off-target effects, CYP450 effects, hERG and cardiac safety, disease models.

title: Zero-order vs first-order kinetics?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Zero-order vs first-order kinetics?
body.back: First-order: constant fraction per time, constant half-life. Zero-order: constant amount per time (saturated), linear fall; phenytoin, ethanol, aspirin.

title: Key half-life facts?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Key half-life facts?
body.back: t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL; rises with Vd, falls with CL; 4-5 t½ ≈ 97% eliminated; doubling the dose adds about one t½ of action.

title: Explain ion trapping for salicylate overdose.
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Explain ion trapping for salicylate overdose.
body.back: Alkaline urine keeps salicylate (pKa 3) ionised (10^(pH-pKa)), preventing tubular reabsorption; used for salicylate and phenobarbital.

title: Steps of drug discovery?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Steps of drug discovery?
body.back: Target identification, molecule design, library screening, SAR modification; then off-target, CYP, hERG and animal-model testing.

title: Phases 1-4 of clinical trials?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Phases 1-4 of clinical trials?
body.back: 1: 20-100 volunteers, safety/dose/PK. 2: 100-300 patients, proof of concept (25% pass). 3: hundreds-thousands, double-blind vs standard. 4: post-marketing surveillance.

title: Parallel vs crossover design?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Parallel vs crossover design?
body.back: Parallel: separate groups get different treatments. Crossover: each subject alternates test drug, placebo and standard; controls for variable disease course.

title: What is the placebo response?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is the placebo response?
body.back: Improvement (up to 30-40%) and even 'side effects' from an inert look-alike, due to expectation and caring attention.

title: PK changes in pregnancy?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: PK changes in pregnancy?
body.back: ↑GFR (faster renal clearance), ↓albumin (↑free fraction, ↑Vd, sometimes ↑hepatic clearance: phenytoin), ↑blood volume/water/fat (↑Vd, longer t½).

title: Factors in placental drug transfer?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Factors in placental drug transfer?
body.back: Lipophilicity, protein binding, molecular weight (< 400-500 Da), pKa (fetal ion trapping), placental metabolism (prednisolone → prednisone).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Collect. Adverse effects reported by patients, health professionals, companies and the literature.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Periodic reporting. Non-serious ADRs such as headache go into periodic safety reports.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Respond. New warnings, label changes, safety announcements or withdrawal.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Review. The regulator analyses data and identifies new, unexpected effects.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Expedited reporting. Serious unexpected ADRs within 15 days; fatal or life-threatening ones within 7 calendar days.

title: Define pharmacovigilance.
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Define pharmacovigilance.
body.back: WHO: the science and activities relating to the detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of adverse drug effects or other drug-related problems.

title: Goals of PV?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Goals of PV?
body.back: Prevent serious drug safety problems, encourage proper drug use, minimise harm from drug use.

title: What does PV monitor after approval?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What does PV monitor after approval?
body.back: Unexpected adverse reactions, drug interactions, risk factors, quality of life, long-term efficacy, cost.

title: List the five 'too's of clinical trials.
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: List the five 'too's of clinical trials.
body.back: Too few (patients), too simple (efficacy only), too median-aged (no children or elderly), too narrow (professional administration), too brief (short duration).

title: Define an adverse drug reaction.
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Define an adverse drug reaction.
body.back: A noxious change suspected to be due to a drug, at normal human doses, requiring treatment, dose reduction or caution in future use.

title: Three steps of PV?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Three steps of PV?
body.back: Collect side-effect information; review clinical data for new signals; respond with warnings, label changes or safety announcements.

title: Reporting timelines for ADRs?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: Reporting timelines for ADRs?
body.back: Serious unexpected: 15 days. Fatal/life-threatening unexpected: 7 calendar days. Non-serious: periodic safety reports.

title: What was the sulfanilamide elixir disaster?
subject: subj:pharma

body.front: What was the sulfanilamide elixir disaster?
body.back: 1937: sulfanilamide dissolved in diethylene glycol, tested only for taste, look and smell; 633 shipments; 107 deaths; led to the 1938 FD&C Act.
